planting.note: Direct-sow in fall for natural cold stratification into soil with consistent summer moisture in sun to part shade.

directions: Split off from the already-present Monarda bradburiana as a distinct species in 2015, this southern Appalachian endemic forms a tidy, mildew-resistant mound of aromatic foliage with a long early-to-midsummer run of white, red-flamed tubular flowers that pollinators work hard. It wants consistent summer moisture rather than the drier conditions tolerated by some relatives, and is a good choice for a partly shaded native pollinator bed where straight Monarda didyma struggles with mildew.

planting.note: Direct-sow in fall into lean, sandy soil in full sun; source only nursery-propagated stock, never wild-collected material, given its imperiled wild status.

directions: A genuinely rare species, globally imperiled and known only from glauconitic sand formations on the Texas-Arkansas border, only formally described in 2011. It forms a clump of lemon-scented, mildew-resistant foliage that can spread to a wide patch in a single season via rhizomes, opening blush pale-yellow flower heads in mid-spring that are a noted bumblebee magnet. Source only nursery-propagated stock to help relieve pressure on wild populations.

planting.note: Direct-sow into deep sandy soil with sharp drainage in full sun; poorly suited to humid climates outside the South Texas and Gulf region.

directions: Endemic to deep sandy soils of the extreme South Texas brush country, this low, heavily branched sub-shrubby perennial has Greek-oregano-scented foliage and can bloom white to pink from March into early winter in its mild native range. It needs sharp drainage and arid conditions to avoid rust and mildew, and is an excellent native-bee and bumblebee plant for xeric South Texas and coastal-plain pollinator gardens.

planting.note: Direct-sow in fall into lean, sandy or loamy, well-drained soil in full sun, mimicking granite-derived Texas Hill Country soils.

directions: A true Texas Hill Country endemic, restricted to granitic sands along the Colorado and Pedernales rivers downstream of the Llano Uplift. It bears white flowers from May through July in woodlands, roadsides, and open fields on sandy or loamy ground, distinguished botanically from relatives by a dense mass of white-silvery hairs closing the calyx mouth. Best suited to lean, sandy, well-drained sites mimicking its granite-derived native soils.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Direct-sow in fall into well-drained soil in full to partial sun with good air circulation to avoid powdery mildew.

directions: Endemic to the Ouachita Mountains of Arkansas, found in dry open woods, fields, meadows, and woodland margins on soils ranging from acidic to basic. White, inch-long, whorled flowers bloom April through July on gray-green stems; it is heat and drought tolerant once established but needs good air circulation to avoid powdery mildew. A documented host plant for numerous caterpillar species and a strong hummingbird and butterfly nectar source.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)
